branch_hypotheses.alternate_path: Board-level concern increases pressure on administration either to justify more fully or to revisit decision, while student activists read elite pressure differently.

branch_hypotheses.alternate_path: Immediate event outcome stays unresolved or fixed while institution shifts focus to policy and governance reform debate.
branch_hypotheses.divergence_signal: Committee formation, review timelines, and declining protest urgency without consensus on the original cancellation.
branch_hypotheses.trigger: No side gains decisive legitimacy, but all sides accept process review as interim outlet.

endpoint_ledger.contradiction_notes: A substitute panel without the same speaker does not satisfy this endpoint.
endpoint_ledger.description: The canceled speaker is later allowed to appear through rescheduling, venue/security modification, or a materially equivalent campus appearance.
endpoint_ledger.label: Speaker reinstated in original or revised form

meta.important_question: Will the university ultimately keep the speaker canceled, reinstate the event in some form, or replace it with substitute programming?

endpoint_ledger.rationale: Reinstatement is a core explicit branch in the scenario and depends on who can revise risk and permission judgments.
realization_criteria: Official university communication confirms a new approved appearance for the same visiting speaker.
Campus venue/security authorization is granted for that appearance.
The event is not merely discussed as a hypothetical or replacement by different participants.
endpoint_ledger.status_basis: Cancellation exists at T0, but faculty and student pressure plus review pathways leave reinstatement plausible.

blockers: Pressure for reinstatement remains stronger than compromise logic
replacement proposal rejected by both factions as illegitimate
endpoint_ledger.contradiction_notes: A pure review announcement without substitute scheduling does not realize this endpoint.
endpoint_ledger.description: The university keeps the speaker canceled while offering a substitute event such as a panel, forum, or alternative speaker program.
endpoint_ledger.label: Cancellation upheld and replacement programming chosen

meta.important_question: Does the institution move into a formal policy/governance review with enough buy-in to stabilize legitimacy?

endpoint_ledger.rationale: This endpoint captures a common administrative compromise mechanism while preserving terminal clarity.
realization_criteria: Administration publicly confirms the original speaker will not appear.
A replacement event is formally scheduled or executed under university sponsorship or approval.
Campus actors treat the substitute as the institution's settled response rather than a temporary placeholder pending reinstatement.
endpoint_ledger.status_basis: Scenario explicitly names replacement event as a plausible path and it offers face-saving flexibility for administrators.

blockers: Hardline factional escalation crowds out process consensus
endpoint_ledger.contradiction_notes: Informal discussion without formal scope, venue, or authorization does not satisfy this endpoint.
endpoint_ledger.description: The dispute shifts into an officially recognized review of event-cancellation, security-assessment, or speaker-governance policy, becoming the main settled institutional outcome.
endpoint_ledger.label: Formal governance or policy review becomes the institution's terminal response

meta.important_question: Do student and faculty reactions remain contained, or do they escalate into sustained visible protest and counter-mobilization?

endpoint_ledger.rationale: The scenario emphasizes governance debate, making review a key terminal institutional outcome distinct from immediate event disposition.
realization_criteria: A committee, senate process, or official review body is announced with scope tied to the cancellation process or policy.
Relevant institutional actors acknowledge the review as the accepted next-step resolution framework.
No immediate reversal is implemented at the moment of review initiation if the original event question remains closed or secondary.
endpoint_ledger.status_basis: Process legitimacy is an explicit focus and offers a convergence pathway when substantive agreement is unavailable.

endpoint_ledger.contradiction_notes: One isolated rally without sustained repetition does not satisfy this endpoint.
endpoint_ledger.description: The campus enters an extended visible conflict cycle in which protests, counter-protests, or repeated public confrontations become the primary settled state.
endpoint_ledger.label: Sustained protest and counter-mobilization dominate the outcome

meta.important_question: Do threatened donor interventions convert into meaningful board or administrative pressure that changes the decision trajectory?

endpoint_ledger.rationale: The scenario explicitly includes protest as a major branch and later evidence can clearly resolve whether mobilization became the dominant outcome.
realization_criteria: Multiple protest actions or organized counter-actions occur across more than one tick/decision moment.
Campus discourse and administrative response are dominated by mobilization management rather than singular event disposition.
Participation extends beyond the original activist core or significantly disrupts normal campus routines.
endpoint_ledger.status_basis: Current conflict is real but not saturated; escalation is plausible if no accepted process develops.

risk_flags.note: Core causal claim rests on undisclosed security information, limiting confidence in trust and legitimacy calibration.
All public actors are kept fictionalized given civic/institutional setting.
Campus population values are realistic defaults rather than corpus-specified counts.
Immediate event control is concentrated in administration and security channels, creating high switching costs for reinstatement.
Donor and board influence may be significant but is mostly private at T0, complicating observability.

simulation_brief.summary: A fictional university has canceled a visiting speaker after a safety assessment. Student groups are split between free-expression and harm-prevention frames, faculty are debating governance and process legitimacy, donors are considering pressure letters, and administrators cite confidential security information. T0 centers on legitimacy, authority constraints, faction alignment, and unresolved paths including reinstatement, replacement programming, protest escalation, or policy review.
uncertainty_notes: Security basis is confidential and not independently verifiable at T0.
Speaker identity, exact campus size, and event timeline are unspecified.
Donor pressure is threatened rather than realized at T0.

sociology_baseline.evidence: Competing frames may persuade moderates only within limited ideological distance.
Quiet plurality likely joins only if visible protest, elite cues, or new disclosures cross a salience threshold.
Many actors are uncertain and may stay quiet under legitimacy ambiguity and peer pressure.
Identity-salient camps likely cluster around existing peer and values networks.
Students may need repeated signals from peers, faculty, and media before public participation.
Scenario focus explicitly includes identity salience and faction split.
Absent new disclosures or protests, broader attention may soften after initial controversy.

sociology_prompt_influences.effect: Raises willingness of organized student groups to interpret events through group protection and principle-defense frames.
Reduces cross-camp trust and increases perceived need to signal side allegiance publicly.
Makes faculty and moderates responsive to transparency, review, and procedural fairness cues rather than only substantive speaker views.
Creates information asymmetry that can either justify caution or intensify suspicion depending on prior trust.
